timeline.body: CIA and MI6 overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh after he nationalized British oil assets, installing the Shah in a coup the CIA did not officially acknowledge until 2013.
The United States built Iran's first nuclear reactor under Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace program — the same nuclear infrastructure Washington would spend decades trying to dismantle.
Iran's Islamic Revolution toppled the US-backed Shah, severed all ties with Israel, and transferred the Israeli embassy in Tehran to the Palestine Liberation Organization.

Iraq invaded Iran with tacit US support, beginning an eight-year war that killed half a million people while Washington supplied Saddam Hussein with satellite intelligence and looked the other way on chemical weapons use.

Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman formed the Gulf Cooperation Council — a security bloc born directly from the fear that the Iranian Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War would spill across the Gulf.

Iran helped found Hezbollah during Israel's invasion of Lebanon, establishing the proxy warfare model — funding, training, and arming allied militias across the region — that would define its strategy for four decades.
Iran and Iraq began attacking each other's oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, striking over 450 vessels by 1988 and turning the Strait of Hormuz into a militarized chokepoint for the first time.

USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard — the United States never formally apologized, and the ship's captain received a Legion of Merit.
An Iranian dissident group revealed secret nuclear sites at Natanz and Arak that Iran had hidden from inspectors, shattering IAEA confidence and triggering a crisis that has never fully resolved.

Iran transmitted a comprehensive negotiation offer to Washington through the Swiss ambassador, proposing talks on its nuclear program, Israel, and Hezbollah — the Bush administration, flush from invading Iraq, never responded.
The Stuxnet worm, built jointly by the US and Israel, destroyed roughly a thousand Iranian centrifuges at Natanz — the first cyberweapon known to physically sabotage another country's infrastructure.

Israeli agents assassinated at least five Iranian nuclear scientists, most using magnetic bombs attached to cars on the streets of Tehran, culminating in the killing of the program's chief architect Mohsen Fakhrizadeh.
Iran and six world powers signed the JCPOA, trading strict limits on uranium enrichment for sanctions relief — the most significant US-Iran diplomatic achievement since before the revolution.
Trump unilaterally withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed maximum-pressure sanctions despite Iran's verified compliance, collapsing the deal and removing Iran's incentive to limit enrichment.

A US drone strike at Baghdad airport killed Qasem Soleimani, commander of Iran's Quds Force and architect of its proxy network across Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen — the most senior foreign military official the US had killed since Admiral Yamamoto in 1943.

The Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco, redrawing the region's alliance structure around a shared view of Iran — not Israel — as the primary threat.
Iran and Israel's decades-long shadow war broke into the open for the first time, with both countries launching direct military strikes against each other's territory.

Iran and Israel fought a 12-day war with direct US military involvement, the most significant open conflict between the two countries in history and the first time American forces engaged Iran in sustained combat.

The Strait of Hormuz narrows to 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passes through it every day, giving Iran a chokepoint over the global economy that no sanctions regime can neutralize.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: Congress passed the Antideficiency Act to prevent federal agencies from spending money not yet appropriated — the obscure fiscal rule that would eventually force millions of federal workers off the job each time Congress missed a funding deadline.

The Posse Comitatus Act barred federal military forces from enforcing domestic law, a principle that erodes each time armed federal agents in tactical gear are deployed in civilian spaces like airports and train stations.

After a wave of hijackings to Cuba, the FAA mandated metal detectors and bag searches at every US airport — but outsourced the screening to private contractors paying near minimum wage with turnover exceeding 100% annually.

Ronald Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and permanently banned them from federal service, establishing the precedent that transportation workers who disrupt operations are expendable regardless of their grievances.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich forced two government shutdowns totaling 27 days over a budget dispute with Bill Clinton, pioneering the shutdown as a deliberate political weapon rather than an accidental funding lapse.
Nineteen hijackers passed through private airport security on September 11, exploiting a system where screeners earned around $6 an hour and routinely failed to detect test weapons in FAA audits.

Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act within two months of the attacks, federalizing all airport screening under a new Transportation Security Administration with over 55,000 employees.
The Homeland Security Act merged 22 federal agencies into the Department of Homeland Security — the largest US government reorganization since the Department of Defense was created in 1947.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement launched with a mandate far broader than the agencies it replaced, combining immigration enforcement with customs investigations and quickly becoming the principal interior enforcement arm of US immigration law.

TSA screeners were explicitly carved out of standard federal employee protections — no collective bargaining, no union representation, and limited appeal rights, despite performing work Congress had just declared essential to national security.

A 16-day government shutdown forced 800,000 federal workers off the job while TSA agents and other workers deemed 'essential' were required to keep showing up with no guarantee of when they would be paid.

A dispute over border wall funding triggered a 35-day government shutdown — the longest in American history — with 420,000 federal employees compelled to work without pay, including the entire TSA screening workforce.
TSA agents earning roughly $36,000 a year went five weeks without paychecks; sick-call rates at some airports spiked past 10% and security wait times at major hubs stretched beyond 90 minutes.

Congress passed the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act guaranteeing back pay after shutdowns — but the law does nothing to prevent the shutdowns themselves or the weeks of financial hardship before paychecks arrive.
DHS finally extended collective bargaining rights to TSA's 60,000 screeners, 21 years after the agency was created — making them the last major federal workforce to gain union representation.
TSA screens roughly 2.5 million passengers daily across 440 airports, making it the single largest point of daily contact between the federal government and the American public.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
